system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search freely for the most promising selective dependencies in the data.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

I'm going through the candidate paralog pairs one by one: RPP25/RPP25L, DNAJC15/DNAJC19, FAM126A/HYCC2, ATP6V0A1/A2, TTC7B/TTC7A, DMXL2/DMXL1, STK39/OXSR1, ATP6V0E2/E1, AGPAT2/AGPAT1, and ACOT9/SUCLA2. Several are already established, DNAJC15/DNAJC19 is still uncertain, and ACOT9/SUCLA2 looks interesting but doesn't seem to be a paralog pair.

Many of these are subtype markers, like MEF2B in lymphoma. Next I want to check how novel the paralog pairs are, and then look at more pages.

input.mechanism: Paralog buffering: ATP6V0E1 and ATP6V0E2 encode alternative e subunits of the V-ATPase V0 sector. When ATP6V0E2 expression is lost, V-ATPase assembly/function depends solely on ATP6V0E1. Seen across squamous/esophagogastric and other lineages (20/23 altered lines strongly dependent).

Paralog buffering in the SOSS single-strand DNA binding complex: hSSB2 (NABP1) and hSSB1 (NABP2) are alternative OB-fold subunits for genome maintenance/replication stress responses; loss of NABP1 makes cells reliant on NABP2. Holds within neuroblastoma, CNS, lung and soft tissue.

Redundant final step of Kennedy-pathway phosphatidylcholine synthesis: CHPT1 and CEPT1 both transfer phosphocholine to DAG; with CHPT1 silenced, PC synthesis depends on CEPT1. 12/13 altered lines strongly dependent; holds when lymphoid lines removed.

Paralog buffering in phosphatidic acid synthesis: AGPAT1 and AGPAT2 acylate lysophosphatidic acid to make PA for glycerolipid synthesis; AGPAT2-silenced lines (neuroblastoma, B-cell, others) require AGPAT1.

Redundant non-canonical nucleotide sanitization: PUDP (HDHD1) dephosphorylates non-canonical nucleoside monophosphates and ITPA hydrolyses ITP/dITP/XTP; with PUDP lost (e.g. Xp22.31 deletion), cells become dependent on ITPA to prevent toxic non-canonical nucleotide incorporation into RNA/DNA.

input.summary: I surveyed the strongest lineage-adjusted biomarker-to-dependency pairs genome-wide. I set aside textbook pairs (TP53 mutation→TP53BP1/USP28, MSI-associated mutations→WRN, SMARCA4→SMARCA2, ARID1A→ARID1B, RPP25→RPP25L, BRAF hotspot→MAP2K1) and pairs that mostly reflect lymphoma or other subtype identity (MEF2B, EBF1, CYB561A3, ACOT9→SUCLA2, ATP6V0A1→ATP6V0A2). I then checked candidates for lineage confounding and searched PubMed. Several PubMed searches failed with rate-limit errors (HTTP 429), including the CHPT1/CEPT1 search before a retry and a broad search for published paralog synthetic-lethality screens. Because of that, the novelty calls are provisional. These are mostly paralog-buffering pairs, which large published paralog screens may already cover, so I give lower confidence on novelty than on replication. I registered five hypotheses and all five replicated, with one-sided p < 0.01 in both held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens. Four are paralog-buffering pairs: ATP6V0E2/E1, NABP1/NABP2, CHPT1/CEPT1 and AGPAT2/AGPAT1. One is a non-paralog pair in nucleotide sanitization: PUDP/ITPA, which had no PubMed hits. Caveats: altered-line counts in the replication sets are small for CHPT1 (6 Broad, 3 Sanger) and AGPAT2 (5 Sanger). CHPT1, AGPAT2 and NABP1 loss is enriched in lymphoid or neuroblastoma lines, though the effects held when I left out one lineage at a time.

findings.claim: Cancer lines that have lost ATP6V0E2 expression depend strongly on its paralog ATP6V0E1, a V-ATPase V0 subunit, across squamous, esophagogastric and other lineages; the effect was about -0.9 in all three datasets.

Lines that have lost NABP1 (hSSB2) are selectively dependent on its paralog NABP2 (hSSB1), part of the SOSS complex; the effect is enriched in neuroblastoma and embryonal CNS tumours but also seen in other lineages.
Lines that have lost CHPT1 depend on CEPT1 for the last step of phosphatidylcholine synthesis; replication rests on few altered lines (6 Broad, 3 Sanger).
Lines that have lost AGPAT2 are selectively dependent on AGPAT1 for making phosphatidic acid; the signal is enriched in neuroblastoma and B-cell lines.
Lines that have lost PUDP (HDHD1) are selectively dependent on ITPA, which may reflect redundant clean-up of non-canonical nucleotides; PubMed returned no reports linking the two genes.

Lines that have lost PUDP (HDHD1) are selectively dependent on ITPA, which may reflect redundant clean-up of non-canonical nucleotides; PubMed returned no reports linking the two genes.

output: Findings recorded.
